card werk-cc-subagents-link-check  [decided]
The lint check fails when werk's own copy of a shipped subagent is not a link
why: werk's own agents must run the same subagent prompts that users get, and that holds only while the repository's folder links to the one shipped definition. A forgotten link or a copy made over a link fails without any sign: the agent is missing when called, or it runs an old prompt. A check at the end of the lint check catches both before a merge, and the merge loop needs no new check.
subtree: 1 card, 1 decided

Claude Code reads subagents from one folder of the repository. werk's own repository needs the shipped subagents there, and their one definition lives elsewhere in werk's source, so the folder holds links to it (#werk-cc-subagents). Two mistakes break that, and neither shows. A shipped subagent has no link: the agent instructions name an agent that the repository lacks, and the failure appears when an agent first calls it. A link is replaced by a plain file with the same name: agents run it, but a later fix to the shipped definition never reaches it, so werk's own agents run a prompt that users do not get.

To catch both before a merge, the lint check ends with a small program that compares the shipped subagents with the folder. It fails when a shipped subagent has no entry, when its entry is a plain file, or when its link points to any file other than the shipped definition. A subagent that only werk's development uses is not shipped, and the program ignores it. The check runs wherever the lint check runs: in the merge loop before a merge, on the clean machine after it, and on demand (#werk-checks). The check needs no new check name.

**What the check is not.** It does not run in a project that werk builds. That project has no folder of links, because werk hands the definitions to each agent when it starts the agent (#werk-agent-subagents). It does not judge whether a prompt is good, only that there is one copy of it. It does not stop anyone from making a copy. It makes a copy fail before the merge, so a copy does not stay unseen.

**Example**

- P, the shipped subagent that builds the options of a fork, defined once in werk's source
- F, P's entry in the repository's subagent folder, a link to that definition
- R, a new shipped subagent that someone has just added
- D, a subagent that only werk's development uses, a plain file in the folder

1. An agent saves a rewritten P as a plain file at F. The link is gone.
2. The lint check runs the comparison. F is a plain file, so the check fails with "P is a copy, not a link". The merge stops.
3. The agent restores the link and makes the edit in P's shipped definition. The comparison passes.
4. Someone adds R with no entry in the folder. The check fails with "R has no link".
5. D is a plain file with no shipped definition. The comparison skips it and nothing happens.

```
shipped definitions            repository's subagent folder
   P ------------------------<------ F   link         -> pass
   R                                  (none)          -> fail: no link
   P ------------------------   F'  plain file        -> fail: a copy
                                  D   plain file, not shipped -> skipped
```

card werk-cc-subagents-definition-shape  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
A shipped subagent is one markdown file that Claude Code and werk both read
why: Claude Code needs a markdown file with a header, and werk needs the same prompt in other projects, where the werk command is not on the command path. One file serves both: the repository links to it, and werk reads it and writes the path into the prompt as it ships it. There is one prompt to fix.

Claude Code reads a subagent from a markdown file: a header that gives the name, a description and the allowed tools, then the prompt. werk ships the same subagents into other projects, and there the prompt cannot say "run the werk command", because werk is not on that project's command path. To avoid two files per subagent, the subagent is defined once, as the markdown file Claude Code reads. The repository's subagent folder links to it (#werk-cc-subagents). When werk ships the subagent, it reads the same file, takes the name, description and tools from the header, and replaces each werk command in the prompt with the full path that werk runs from (#werk-agent-subagents). Inside werk's own checkout the link serves the file unchanged, so the command reads as written.

**Example**

- P "prototyper", a shipped subagent. Its prompt tells it to run werk's command that builds one prototype per option.
- C, Claude Code in werk's own repository
- X, another project where werk starts an agent that needs P

1. C opens P through the repository's link. The file is served as written, and the prompt names the werk command. C runs it.
2. A fix to P's prompt is saved in the one file. C sees the fix at its next call.
3. werk starts an agent in X. It reads the same file and takes the name, description and tools from the header.
4. In the prompt, werk replaces the werk command with the full path of the werk it runs from. The agent in X can run it.
5. A prompt with no werk command passes through unchanged.

```
one file: P (header + prompt)
   |
   |-- link ------------> repository's subagent folder -> C   prompt as written
   |
   '-- read at run time -> header kept, command -> path -> agent in X
```

       why: the path substitution applies when the definitions travel with the instructions
  -> refines         werk-cc-subagents  A subagent that werk ships has one definition, and werk's own repository links to it

why: A person copies a printed command into a shell. A printed command is a command that werk shows to a person to copy: the next step after a refused change, or a usage line. To avoid a different first word on every machine, werk starts every printed command with the word werk. It does not read the name of the file that runs. The install puts the executable on the path as werk (#werk-dist-channel). A person who downloads a release file directly names it werk and places it on the path.

When werk runs from a source checkout, the printed command also starts with werk. An agent prompt and a child process use the same full command from one shared source, and never a runtime name with a source path.

Example

- Command "werk": the executable that the install placed on the path
- Card "checkout-retry": a proposal that waits for accept

Steps

1. Maria installs werk. The shell now finds the command werk.
2. Maria opens a change that werk refuses.
3. werk prints the next step: "werk accept checkout-retry". Maria pastes it and it runs.
4. A developer runs werk from a checkout. The printed line is the same: it starts with "werk".
5. A person who runs the file under another name sees the same printed line, and the shell does not find werk. The fix is on the path, not in werk.

  how werk runs     printed command
  ----------------  -------------------------
  installed         werk accept <card>
  from a checkout   werk accept <card>
  any file name     werk accept <card>

Every agent that can write to the map reads the werk agent instructions, in any project
why: An agent follows only the rules it reads. A build pass runs in the project's own repository, and the project's own instruction files know nothing about the map. So werk gives its instructions to each agent it starts.
subtree: 5 cards, 5 decided

Werk keeps one instruction text for agents: how to keep the map current, how to propose and word a card, and how to tag who decides. The text is about any project werk works on, not about werk itself. Werk adds it to the system prompt of every agent it starts that can write to the map: the chat pane agent, each build pass, and the plan writers. The text names the werk command line by the path werk runs from, so its commands work in any repository.

An agent with a narrow contract does not get the text, because the text would contradict that contract. A sample agent may not write to the map. The diagram agents edit the product diagram, and the text forbids that. A model call with no tools cannot act on the map at all.

When the project is werk itself, its own instruction file already includes the text, so werk does not add it a second time.
